title: 1 Samuel 20:35–42
context: The next morning, Jonathan carries out the arrow signal that tells David he must flee, sends the boy back to the city, and meets David for a final farewell. They weep together, and Jonathan sends David away in peace, recalling their oath that the LORD is between them and their offspring forever. The chapter closes as David departs and Jonathan returns to the city. Both traditions read the scene as shared ground about covenant friendship.

verses.text: In the morning, Jonathan went out into the field at the time appointed with David, and a little boy with him.
verses.arminianNotes:
In the morning, Jonathan goes to the field at the appointed time with a young boy. The signal plan is put into action.

Arminian readers see Jonathan keeping his word faithfully despite the cost.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan arrives as promised. The boy will unknowingly carry the message.

Reformed readers see faithfulness in small details. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the quiet, poignant tone of the final scene after the anger of the meal.

verses.text: He said to his boy, “Run, find now the arrows which I shoot.” As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan tells the boy to run and find the arrows, and shoots an arrow beyond him. The signal for danger is given.

Arminian readers see Jonathan carrying out the painful message he had hoped not to send.
verses.reformedNotes:
The arrow beyond the boy means David must flee. The plan works as arranged.

Reformed readers see providence working through ordinary actions. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with the simple action carrying heavy meaning for the two friends.

verses.text: When the boy had come to the place of the arrow which Jonathan had shot, Jonathan cried after the boy, and said, “Isn’t the arrow beyond you?”
verses.arminianNotes:
When the boy reaches the arrow, Jonathan calls, “Isn’t the arrow beyond you?” The code words are spoken.

Arminian readers see Jonathan faithfully delivering bad news as promised. He does not soften the signal.
verses.reformedNotes:
The words match the signal agreed in verse 22. David hears what he needs to know.

Reformed readers see covenant faithfulness in action. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, with the agreed phrase now confirming that David must leave.

verses.text: Jonathan cried after the boy, “Go fast! Hurry! Don’t delay!” Jonathan’s boy gathered up the arrows, and came to his master.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan shouts to the boy to hurry and not delay; the boy gathers the arrows and returns. The urgency may also be meant for David.

Arminian readers see Jonathan’s concern for David’s quick escape.
verses.reformedNotes:
The commands to hurry fit the boy’s task but may also address David. Interpreters suggest a double meaning.

Reformed readers hold the suggestion lightly. Both traditions read this as shared ground, without pressing the possible double meaning beyond what the text supports.

verses.text: But the boy didn’t know anything. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter.
verses.arminianNotes:
The boy knows nothing; only Jonathan and David understand. The secret is kept.

Arminian readers see the plan protecting the innocent boy as well as David. No one else is drawn into danger.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator emphasizes that the message was private. The boy is not involved in the danger.

Reformed readers see prudence that protects others. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note how carefully the friends guard their communication in a dangerous court.

verses.text: Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy, and said to him, “Go, carry them to the city.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan gives his weapons to the boy and sends him back to the city. The friends are now alone.

Arminian readers see Jonathan making room for a final, private farewell.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sending the boy away allows the meeting the plan had seemed to rule out. Jonathan chooses to see David once more.

Reformed readers see love taking a risk for a last goodbye. Both traditions read this as shared ground about faithful friendship.

verses.text: As soon as the boy was gone, David arose out of the south, and fell on his face to the ground, and bowed himself three times. They kissed one another and wept with one another, and David wept the most.
verses.arminianNotes:
David comes out from the south, bows three times, and the two friends kiss and weep, David weeping the most. Their parting is deeply emotional.

Arminian readers see honest grief in a friendship marked by covenant love.
verses.reformedNotes:
David honors Jonathan with repeated bowing. The tears express love and loss.

Reformed readers see godly friendship grieving separation. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground and treat the scene with respect, as a farewell between covenant friends in a time of danger.

verses.text: Jonathan said to David, “Go in peace, because we have both sworn in the LORD’s name, saying, ‘The LORD is between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.’ ” He arose and departed; and Jonathan went into the city.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan tells David to go in peace, recalling their oath that the LORD is between them and their offspring forever. Then they part, and Jonathan returns to the city.

Arminian readers see a covenant freely sworn and faithfully remembered.
verses.reformedNotes:
The farewell restates the covenant of verse 23 and extends it to their descendants. The LORD is its witness.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness underlying human promises. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and 2 Samuel 9 shows David later keeping faith with Jonathan’s house.
